name: Moss Green
lede: Moss green is a muted yellowish green named for the plant, and the name has also been used for a pigment whose identity the books cannot agree on.

sections.title: What the dictionaries say
sections.body:
Paterson defines moss green as a yellowy green, an olivy green, and lists moss-grey as a greeny grey beside it [1]. The plant itself is listed only as a shade of green [1]. The swatch here is a medium, slightly yellowish green, and the nearest named neighbors in the app are [[moss]], [[moss-olive]] and [[olive-green]] [2], and the pigment name it is sometimes tied to is [[emerald-green]].

It appears in Maerz and Paul's color dictionary of 1930, the earliest record in our sources [2]. Moss is a good example of a color word that is easier to see than to define: the green of a damp wall is brighter than the green of dried moss in a wood, and both are called moss.

sections.title: A pigment name that points two ways
sections.body:
In the Pigment Compendium, Moss green is a synonym of two different pigments, depending on who is asked [3]. Fiedler and Bayard list it, in 1997, as one of the less common names for emerald green, an arsenic-based green [3]. Mayer, in 1991, treats it as a name for chrome green instead [3]. The books disagree, and the compendium does not resolve it [3].

A list of green pigment names in the same book includes moss green beside Brunswick green, leaf green and viridian [4]. Baty's reference chart of natural pigments also lists a Moss Green among its paint-maker colour names, in rows beside oxide of chromium and olive green [5]. In short, the name was never tied to one agreed substance.

sections.title: Seen in cloth
sections.body: Finlay, looking through tweed samples, records a pink-moss-green among the bright notes in a drawer of mostly browns and greys [6]. For a viewer, it is a reminder to look for this middle green in wool and lichen, not only in paint.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a moss green of this swatch appears in 84 paintings, 0.35 per cent, as photographed; the stricter within-painting count finds it in 36 [7]. It is rarer than 55 per cent of the named colors, and it plays an accent in 58 per cent of those 36 paintings [7]. It peaks in the 1900s, found in 0.7 per cent of 1,674 paintings from that decade, 3.9 times the rate expected from the same museums [7]. France is the country where it is over-represented, 2.4 times expected, in 17 of 3,443 paintings [7]. The earliest match, 1512, is a painting by Andrea del Sarto, well before the name's first record in 1930, so it is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test [7].
